topics.name: Road signs and signals
topics.summary: Read junction signals and know when another instruction takes priority.
lesson: Read the whole junction as you approach. Find the stop line, the signal that controls your movement and the space available on the far side. A green signal still requires a clear, safe path.

If a steady amber appears and you can stop safely, stop before the line. When it first appears and you are already too close to stop safely, the RSA allows you to continue. A filter arrow applies to the direction it points.
Watch for Garda directions when someone is controlling traffic in person. Also check for conflicting pedestrians, cyclists and traffic before moving off, including alongside your cab.

sources.section: Section 7, Traffic lights and signals by motorists

topics.name: Rules of the road
topics.summary: Plan enough space to clear junctions and manoeuvre safely.
lesson: At a stop sign, come to a complete stop at the line if there is one. Use the stop to look for people crossing and traffic you need to yield to, including any obscured approach.

Before entering a yellow box, check that your entire vehicle can clear it. When turning right, there is a limited exception for waiting for oncoming traffic where you can avoid blocking traffic with right of way. At railway or tramway boxes, wait until you can clear the box without stopping.
Think about pedestrians already crossing the road you are turning into. An indicator communicates your plan. You still need a clear path and time to complete the manoeuvre safely.

sources.section: Section 9, Junctions and yellow box junctions

topics.name: Vehicle checks and defects
topics.summary: Use the correct walk-around checklist and follow up defects.
lesson: Use the CVRT checklist for the vehicle type. A check before public-road use helps catch faults before departure. The owner’s maintenance programme also includes planned preventative checks.
Know who receives the defect report. Record what you found, when you found it and any temporary measures taken. The report lets the maintenance team track what needs to be inspected and repaired.

If a potentially dangerous fault develops during a journey, stop as soon as you can in a safe place. Keep the vehicle out of use until a suitably qualified person has inspected the defect and repaired it where necessary.

sources.section: What do daily walk around checks entail?; recording and detection of defects

topics.name: Loads and load security
topics.summary: Assess load distribution and restraint as separate checks.
lesson: Assess how the load is distributed and how it is held in place. The load can affect stability even when it stays on the vehicle. Discuss the load plan with the operator or loading team before departure.

Check the applicable gross and axle limits for the particular combination. A satisfactory gross weight can coexist with too much weight on one axle. Partial unloading can change which axle is most heavily loaded.

Use the operator’s load-specific restraint procedure and training. Reassess the arrangement after drops or changes. If there is doubt about whether the load can be carried safely, resolve it before driving.

sources.section: Frequently asked questions, general laws on securing a load

topics.name: Trailers and couplings
topics.summary: Understand what the final departure checks are meant to verify.
lesson: Before coupling or uncoupling, use the procedure for the specific tractor, trailer and coupling. Choose a suitable place and account for trailer movement, trailer support and people nearby.

For a fifth-wheel combination, the checks include confirming that the locking mechanism is secure, the air and electrical connections are made and the landing gear is stowed before departure. Follow the sequence in your vehicle and operator procedures.
Complete the combination’s walk-around after coupling. Include the trailer lights and confirm the checks required by the operator before you take the combination onto the road.

sources.section: What do daily walk around checks entail?

topics.name: Tachographs and drivers’ hours
topics.summary: Identify which rules apply before calculating driving or break time.
lesson: Start with the operation and vehicle. Articles 2 and 3 set the scope and exemptions, including an exemption from this regulation for regular passenger services on routes of 50 km or less. Other requirements can still apply.

Under Article 6, the standard daily driving limit is nine hours, with an extension to ten hours at most twice in a week. The weekly driving limit is 56 hours and the total for two consecutive weeks is 90 hours.

Article 7 generally requires at least 45 minutes of break after four and a half hours of driving unless a rest period begins. The standard split is at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30. Occasional passenger services have a separate split option: two breaks of at least 15 minutes each that together meet the 45-minute requirement. Check the scope and record requirements before relying on a special provision.

topics.name: Braking and stopping distances
topics.summary: Leave room for the driver and the vehicle to react.
lesson: Stopping takes space before and after the brakes are applied. The driver needs time to notice and respond to the hazard, then vehicle response and grip affect the distance needed to stop.

Measure following time from a fixed roadside point. The RSA’s two-second rule is a minimum in dry conditions. Increase the space in rain and allow still more when visibility or grip is severely reduced.

Manage speed so you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear. Use the RSA car stopping-distance examples to understand the effect of conditions and speed. A heavy vehicle’s stopping distance depends on its own condition, loading and available grip.

sources.section: Section 8, Driving safely in traffic and stopping distance

topics.name: Risk and eco-driving
topics.summary: Spot developing hazards early and keep your inputs smooth.
lesson: Look well ahead for signals, queues and places where road users may enter your path. If traffic is slowing ahead, planning early gives you time to ease off and brake progressively.
Smooth acceleration and forward planning can improve fuel use while leaving more time to respond to hazards. Allow enough space ahead so you can respond to traffic changes gradually.
Treat fighting sleep as a reason to stop. Pull into a safe place. A rest plan starts before the journey, especially if you are working shifts or starting early.

topics.name: Dangerous goods (ADR)
topics.summary: Recognise when specialist dangerous-goods guidance is needed.
lesson: ADR covers the carriage of dangerous goods by road. Training and certification depend on the goods and how they are carried. HSA guidance distinguishes tank operations from packaged goods and describes relevant exemptions.

Before accepting a load that may fall under ADR, ask the operator or dangerous-goods safety adviser to confirm the classification, operation and applicable requirements. Use the current HSA guidance and the rules for the actual load.

topics.name: Bus passenger safety
topics.summary: Build a safe routine for boarding, alighting and moving off.
lesson: At an authorised stop, secure the stationary vehicle before opening the doors and check the door area. Watch for people approaching late or standing in blind spots.

Check that boarding and alighting are complete before closing the doors. Allow time for passengers who need it to get settled and confirm that a wheelchair user is safely accommodated before moving away.
Include ramps or lifts where fitted, handrails and exits in the applicable pre-use checks. Use the operator’s accessibility and vehicle procedures for the equipment on your bus.

sources.section: Module 6.3 Session 2, Checking safety equipment and Boarding and alighting (p. 27)

topics.name: Vehicle dimensions and weight
topics.summary: Match the actual combination and its load to the route.
lesson: Identify the combination, its axle layout and its loaded dimensions. Look up limits for that configuration in current RSA guidance. Limits depend on the vehicle and its design, so a number from another combination can be misleading.
Check route restrictions, especially height, width and weight limits. If a restriction cannot be met, plan a suitable route before you reach it.
For an abnormal indivisible load, check the RSA permit guidance before moving it. The issuing authority can depend on the dimensions and the roads used.

sources.section: Maximum permitted weights and dimensions; Abnormal and indivisible loads

topics.name: Breakdowns and emergencies
topics.summary: Recognise when to seek help and where to wait safely.
lesson: An emergency breakdown is a reason to use the motorway hard shoulder when you can reach it safely. Once stopped, use hazard lights and call for help from a safe location.

If everyone can leave safely, wait on the embankment side behind the crash barrier where available. If you cannot follow the safe-exit advice, the RSA advises staying in the vehicle with your seat belt secured and hazards on.

Tell responders the direction of travel and the location. Motorway location markers, where available, can help. In a tunnel, check the signs and use the emergency station phone to reach the tunnel operator in a breakdown or crash.

sources.section: Section 11, Motorway breakdowns and tunnel breakdown or crash
Motorway safety campaign, emergency stops and roadside phones

questions.question: On a delivery run, the steady amber comes on while you still have ample distance to stop smoothly. What should you do?
options: Proceed because the light has not turned red.
Stop before the stop line.
Stop after the line if the pedestrian crossing is empty.
questions.explanation: Stop before the line when you can do so safely. The exception applies if you were already too close to stop safely when amber first appeared.

evidence.rationale: Stop before the line when you can do so safely. The exception applies if you were already too close to stop safely when amber first appeared.
evidence.scope: Steady amber at a signal-controlled junction.

questions.question: A Garda managing a junction gives you a clear signal to stop while your traffic light is green. Which instruction controls your movement?
options: The Garda’s stop signal.
The green light until it changes.
Whichever signal was given first.
questions.explanation: A Garda directing traffic takes priority over traffic lights.

evidence.rationale: A Garda directing traffic takes priority over traffic lights.
evidence.scope: A Garda is actively controlling traffic.

questions.question: Your coach is in the left-turn lane. A green left arrow is lit alongside the red main signal, and the turn is clear. What does the arrow permit?
options: Driving straight through the junction.
Waiting until the main light turns green before turning.
Turning left if it remains safe.
questions.explanation: A green filter arrow permits the indicated movement when safe, even alongside a red main signal.

evidence.rationale: A green filter arrow permits the indicated movement when safe, even alongside a red main signal.
evidence.scope: A green arrow controlling the left turn.

questions.question: The traffic lights at a junction are out of order. You are approaching the control line in a rigid truck. What does the RSA advise?
options: Treat the failed signal as a green light if you are on the wider road.
Stop at the control line, then proceed safely while yielding to traffic with right of way.
Slow down and continue without stopping if the first lane is clear.
questions.explanation: Stop at the line first. Check the whole junction and yield as required before proceeding.

evidence.rationale: Stop at the line first. Check the whole junction and yield as required before proceeding.
evidence.scope: Failed signals without a Garda directing traffic.

questions.question: Flashing red lights are showing at an automated railway crossing. The barrier has yet to close. What should you do?
options: Go through before the barrier starts moving.
Continue if you can see both ways along the tracks.
Stop safely before the crossing.
questions.explanation: Flashing red at the level crossing tells you to stop, regardless of the barrier’s position.

evidence.rationale: Flashing red at the level crossing tells you to stop, regardless of the barrier’s position.
evidence.scope: Active flashing red signals at an automated railway crossing.

questions.question: You are going straight through a yellow box. The lights are green, but the queue beyond leaves room for only the front of your vehicle. Where should you wait?
options: Inside the box with only the cab across.
Before the box until the full vehicle can clear it.
Inside the box as long as the traffic light stays green.
questions.explanation: Wait before entering. You need space to clear the box without stopping when going straight.

evidence.rationale: Wait before entering. You need space to clear the box without stopping when going straight.
evidence.scope: Straight-ahead movement, so the right-turn exception does not apply.

questions.question: You approach a stop sign with a marked line at the exit from an industrial estate. The main road appears empty. What is required at the line?
options: Slow to a crawl and continue if nobody is visible.
Stop only if another vehicle is approaching.
Come to a complete stop before continuing when safe.
questions.explanation: The stop sign requires a full stop even when the road looks empty.

evidence.rationale: The stop sign requires a full stop even when the road looks empty.
evidence.scope: A stop sign with a marked stop line.

questions.question: You are turning left at a junction and see a pedestrian already crossing the road you are entering. What should you do?
options: Wait and yield to the pedestrian.
Continue because you started indicating first.
Pass behind the pedestrian as soon as there is space for your front wheels.
questions.explanation: Give way to people already crossing at a junction before completing the turn.

evidence.rationale: Give way to people already crossing at a junction before completing the turn.
evidence.scope: The pedestrian has already started crossing.

questions.question: On a clear two-lane motorway you have finished overtaking, and there is ample room in the left lane. Where should you drive next?
options: Stay in the right lane until approaching an exit.
Return to the left lane when safe.
Use either lane according to which has the better road surface.
questions.explanation: Use the left lane for normal motorway driving. Return to it once the overtake is complete and it is safe.

evidence.section: Motorway safety campaign, rules of the road
evidence.rationale: Use the left lane for normal motorway driving. Return to it once the overtake is complete and it is safe.
evidence.scope: Normal driving, left lane clear and available.

questions.question: You signal to change lanes but a vehicle in the destination lane is still alongside your rear quarter. What should you do?
options: Move over gradually so it can slow down.
Move as soon as your indicator has flashed three times.
Hold your lane until a safe gap opens.
questions.explanation: An indicator communicates intent. Check that the lane change is safe before moving across.

evidence.rationale: An indicator communicates intent. Check that the lane change is safe before moving across.
evidence.scope: Ordinary lane change with another vehicle alongside.

questions.question: How can you measure your following gap in seconds on a dry road?
options: Count from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed marker until you reach it.
Count from when you pass a marker until the vehicle ahead passes the next marker.
Divide the distance to the vehicle ahead by the posted limit.
questions.explanation: Use the same fixed point for both vehicles. The elapsed time is the following gap.

evidence.rationale: Use the same fixed point for both vehicles. The elapsed time is the following gap.
evidence.scope: Measuring the gap on a dry road.

questions.question: Steady rain wets the road as you follow another vehicle. How should you adjust the RSA dry-road two-second benchmark?
options: Keep it if your vehicle has ABS.
Reduce it to make the other vehicle easier to see.
Double the benchmark and increase it further if conditions demand.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises doubling the dry-road following distance in wet weather. Severe conditions can call for more space.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises doubling the dry-road following distance in wet weather. Severe conditions can call for more space.
evidence.scope: Wet-road benchmark, adjusted for actual conditions.

questions.question: A bend hides the road ahead and you are travelling below the posted speed limit. How should you select your speed?
options: Use the posted limit because the road is dry.
Use a speed that lets you stop within the road you can see is clear.
Match the speed of the vehicle ahead without considering visibility.
questions.explanation: The visible, clear distance has to be enough to stop safely. A posted limit alone cannot tell you that.

evidence.rationale: The visible, clear distance has to be enough to stop safely. A posted limit alone cannot tell you that.
evidence.scope: Restricted forward visibility.

questions.question: Two otherwise identical journeys approach a hazard at the same speed. On one, the driver takes longer to recognise it. What changes before braking starts?
options: The vehicle covers more distance before braking.
The vehicle covers less distance before braking.
Only the distance after braking can change.
questions.explanation: While the driver is still recognising the hazard and reacting, the vehicle keeps moving.

evidence.section: Section 8, Stopping distance for cars, perception and reaction time
evidence.rationale: While the driver is still recognising the hazard and reacting, the vehicle keeps moving.
evidence.scope: Compares the distance before braking at the same speed. No car-specific distances are used.

questions.question: Two otherwise identical vehicles are travelling at the same speed and their drivers react at the same moment. Which change can reduce braking grip?
options: The driver choosing an earlier time to start the shift.
The vehicle behind leaving a larger gap.
A slippery surface under the tyres.
questions.explanation: Available tyre grip affects braking capability. A slippery surface reduces the grip available.

evidence.section: Section 8, Stopping distance for cars and skidding
evidence.rationale: Available tyre grip affects braking capability. A slippery surface reduces the grip available.
evidence.scope: General grip principle without vehicle-specific stopping figures.

questions.question: You see a queue building well ahead on a straight road. Which approach best demonstrates forward planning?
options: Hold speed until close to the queue, then brake firmly.
Ease off early and slow progressively.
Accelerate into the free space before braking.
questions.explanation: Spotting the queue early gives you time to ease off and avoid late, harsh braking.

evidence.rationale: Spotting the queue early gives you time to ease off and avoid late, harsh braking.
evidence.scope: A developing queue far enough ahead for gradual deceleration.

questions.question: On the last leg of a journey you find yourself fighting sleep. What is the first priority?
options: Open a window and complete the leg without stopping.
Arrange a break after the last stop.
Pull into a safe place and stop driving.
questions.explanation: The RSA’s first step for tired drivers is to park safely. Plan a break before continuing.

evidence.rationale: The RSA’s first step for tired drivers is to park safely. Plan a break before continuing.
evidence.scope: Immediate response to fighting sleep.

questions.question: After leaving a patch of dense fog, you are driving in clear weather again. What should you do with the fog lights?
options: Turn them off.
Leave them on until the next stop.
Leave them on if another vehicle is behind you.
questions.explanation: Switch off fog lights in clear weather. They can dazzle other drivers.

evidence.rationale: Switch off fog lights in clear weather. They can dazzle other drivers.
evidence.scope: Conditions have cleared and there is no falling snow.

questions.question: The lights change and you can move off safely in a coach. Which technique follows the RSA eco-driving guidance?
options: Build high revs while stationary to move off faster.
Pull away smoothly with progressive accelerator input.
Accelerate hard initially and then coast to settle speed.
questions.explanation: Smooth, progressive acceleration avoids unnecessary engine revs and abrupt changes in speed.

evidence.rationale: Smooth, progressive acceleration avoids unnecessary engine revs and abrupt changes in speed.
evidence.scope: Normal departure in a coach when safe to move off.

questions.question: Heavy rain starts while your truck’s cruise control is active. What does the RSA recommend?
options: Disengage cruise control and manage speed directly.
Keep cruise control on but lower the setting.
Use cruise control until standing water is visible.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises avoiding cruise control in heavy rain because it can reduce control and affect your reaction to hazards.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises avoiding cruise control in heavy rain because it can reduce control and affect your reaction to hazards.
evidence.scope: Heavy rain, even without visible standing water.

questions.question: Following a motorway breakdown, you and your occupants can exit safely and there is a crash barrier next to the hard shoulder. Where should you wait for help?
options: Just in front of the vehicle on the shoulder.
Between the vehicle and the carriageway.
Well behind the barrier on the embankment side.
questions.explanation: Wait away from the live traffic area, behind the crash barrier where available.

evidence.rationale: Wait away from the live traffic area, behind the crash barrier where available.
evidence.scope: Everyone can safely leave and get behind the barrier.

questions.question: You have broken down on a motorway and cannot safely follow the RSA advice to leave the vehicle. How should you wait while getting help?
options: Remain belted in the vehicle with hazard lights on.
Wait unbelted so you can move more quickly.
Stand beside the vehicle nearest to live traffic.
questions.explanation: When it is unsafe to follow the exit advice, the RSA advises staying belted inside with the hazards on.

evidence.rationale: When it is unsafe to follow the exit advice, the RSA advises staying belted inside with the hazards on.
evidence.scope: Safe exit advice cannot be followed.

questions.question: From a safe place you report a motorway breakdown. Which information from a roadside location marker is especially useful?
options: The speed limit for the road.
The location reference and direction of travel.
The permitted gross weight of your vehicle.
questions.explanation: The location reference and direction help responders find the correct stretch of road.

evidence.section: Section 11, Location reference indicators and markings
evidence.rationale: The location reference and direction help responders find the correct stretch of road.
evidence.scope: A location marker is visible from a safe place.

questions.question: Your vehicle has stopped following a breakdown in a tunnel. You can safely reach an emergency station. Which phone should you use to alert the tunnel operator?
options: The tunnel emergency station phone.
A passenger’s phone to call the next toll plaza.
A phone at the first service area outside the tunnel.
questions.explanation: The emergency station phone puts you in contact with the tunnel operator.

evidence.section: Section 11, Tunnels, Breakdown or a crash
evidence.rationale: The emergency station phone puts you in contact with the tunnel operator.
evidence.scope: You can safely reach a tunnel emergency station.

questions.question: You miss your motorway exit while trying to reach a service area. What is the safe way to correct the route?
options: Reverse along the hard shoulder to the exit.
Turn at the next gap in the central barrier.
Continue to a suitable exit ahead.
questions.explanation: Motorway rules prohibit turning or reversing. Continue ahead until you can leave by an exit.

evidence.section: Motorway safety campaign, rules of the road
evidence.rationale: Motorway rules prohibit turning or reversing. Continue ahead until you can leave by an exit.
evidence.scope: Ordinary missed exit, without an emergency or Garda instruction.
